subsubtopic: SCIENTIFIC GENDER SELECTION-STUDY OF ISSUES URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because male and female sperm determinant differ, it is now possible to choose whether a boy or girl will be born. For those for whom a 50-50 chance has produced the reality of several children of the same sex, this technology can provide a happier balance, and for that it is to be welcomed. But all may not be well as gender selection kits appear on the shelves of corner drug stores.
Dare we ask whether a mechanism produced by billions of years of evolution to ensure equal proportion of males and females and the perpetuation of the species should now be replaced by the same kind of preference as that for the colour of a new car?
Does not the establishment of gender selection clinics by oh, so humanitarian, multinational corporations in the Third World suggest a new and dramatically effective means of birth control, namely, the elimination of female births?
Are not the kind of ethical and political questions raised by science in the service of personal choice in a narcissistic age as momentous as those for science in the service of war? And is it not time for us to weigh these questions and implications of our creativity, and act to preserve our humanity? Remember, a coin that always turns up heads means someone is always the loser.

December 17, 1986

Mr. Speaker, this past week marked the anniversary of one of the most significant dates in Canadian constitutional history. I am referring to the passage of the Statute of Westminster passed 55 years ago in December, 1931. In the long constitutional development of this country, that date is as significant as any other.
After the Statute of Westminster, we can say that Canada truly became an independent country. The document confirmed that no legislation passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom would apply to Canada unless expressly authorized by Canada's Parliament. By 1931 the country had come a long way since that day in 1791 when Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe opened the first Legislature of Upper Canada in Niagara-on-the-Lake.
The Statute of Westminster did not, however, sever our allegiance to the Crown, and that is why it was appropriate that the Union Jack flew over government buildings again last week. As one of the local newspapers in my riding, The Niagara Advance, indicated: "The royal standard Union Jack was being flown ... in recognition of Canada's allegiance to the Crown and membership in the Commonwealth of Nations".

THE LATE HONOURABLE SENATOR JEAN-PAUL DESCHATELETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago, Senator Jean-Paul Deschatelets died in Montreal after a long illness. I wish to pay tribute to this public figure who for many years played a major role on the federal political scene, first as a Member of the House of Commons, then as Minister and later as Senator.
I had the privilege of working closely with him during those years and was able to appreciate his exceptional qualities as a humanist. He was the soul of integrity, and those who knew him well will remember him as a philosopher in politics. One is tempted to ask what on earth he was doing in politics. I think he even asked himself that question on occasion. In any case, he always remained faithful to his roots and to his deepest convictions.
We have lost a patriot, and speaking on my own behalf, on behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal Party and especially the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), I wish to extend our sincere condolences to Mrs. Deschatelets and the family.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has said that environmental issues are not part of the free trade negotiations with the United States. Unfortunately, life is not that simple. Whatever either party to the negotiations wants to have on the table is on the table, whether the other party likes it or not. We have already seen that the Americans may consider our social programs to be a government subsidy to Canadian business. There is no reason to believe they will not think the same about our environmental programs.
For example, the Americans could consider government sponsored reforestation programs or pollution abatement programs to be non-tariff trade barriers which we should bargain away. Or, where Canadian environmental laws are weak, we could be locking ourselves into a situation in which they would have to remain weak.
At the moment these environmental dimensions of the free trade initiatives are being overlooked by the federal negotiators. No environmentalists sit on Canada's free trade negotiating team, nor are they among Simon Reisman's 85 staff people or his 54 advisers. There is no commitment on the part of the

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in yesterday's edition of La Presse we learned about the existence of a common front made up of representatives of the business, political and scientific communities, and dedicated to the promotion of Bill C-22 dealing with drug patents.
Such prestigious personalities as Mrs. Manon Vennat, President of the Montreal Board of Trade, Mr. Marcel Daoust, President of the Montreal Chamber of Commerce, and Dr. Jacques Gagne, Dean of the faculty of Pharmacology of Montreal University, have publicly indicated their support for this Bill.
These people believe that the 10 years period of exclusive right granted to manufacturers is not only essential to recognize copyrights but represents for them bare minimum.
The future legislation will make it possible for the Canadian pharmaceutical industry to reach new levels of prosperity. In the Montreal region alone, investments up to $200 million, out of an expected total of $500 million, have already been announced and will create hundreds of high-tech jobs.
Everybody warmly supports this Bill. Apparently, only Members of the Opposition are unable to see its potential benefits.

Mr. Speaker, the depletion of the ozone layer, the greenhouse effect and climatic change, and the long-range transport of acidic and toxic substances are interrelated and cause man's contamination of the atmosphere. A new approach and ethic toward discharging wastes and chemical materials into the air must be adopted on an international scale.
A number of substances, including chlorofluorocarbons, have major impacts on climate and the ozone layer. Chlorofluorocarbons are used in refrigeration, solvents and foam insulation, as spray can propellants, and in fast food containers. Identified as a source of chlorine in the stratosphere, they
contribute to a chemical reaction which is eroding the ozone layer. Scientists say that on average a drop of 1 per cent in the ozone layer means a 4 per cent jump in skin cancer rates.
Canada should take the initiative of urging other nations to control and reduce the use of chlorofluorocarbons, companies should be urged to limit their use, and their disposal should be carefully handled. The ozone layer must be protected to protect human health.

speechtext:
I would like to bring to the attention of Hon. Members that a resolution has been passed in the Legislative Assembly of Ontario concerning the Canadian Constitution. That particular communication has been sent to the Speaker.
In bringing that communication to the attention of all Hon. Members I shall read out the formal parts in a moment, but I want it clearly understood that this communication from the Legislative Assembly of Ontario is by way of information and does not initiate any process within this Chamber.
I have the honour to inform the House that I have received a communication from the Hon. Hugh Edighoffer, Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario, transmitting to this House a resolution adopted by the Legislative Assembly.
The motion reads:
Resolved, That this House authorizes that a Proclamation be issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada amending Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to read as follows:
7. Everyone has the right to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice,
and urges that the Senate and the House of Commons and the Legislative Assemblies of the other provinces do likewise.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday December 16, consideration of Bill C-23, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and a related Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs; and motions Nos. 7 and 14 (Mr. Garneau) (p. 2178-2179) and motions Nos. 8 and 15 (Mr. Cassidy) (p. 2179).

Mr. Speaker, yes, I intend to finish what I have to say about Motion No. 7 and then proceed with Motion No. 14. The purpose of Motion No. 7 was to reduce, from seven years to three, the period during which a taxpayer who paid the minimum tax will be able to recover that payment, and my point was that if a taxpayer is given seven years to recover the minimum tax he
Income Tax Act
paid in a given year, we might as well not adopt this legislation, because in the final instance, no one is going to be stupid enough to have to pay this minimum tax.
I see this as a useless complication of our tax system, since everyone should be able to recover this tax.
Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 14 concerns an equally basic aspect of the minimum tax. The tax was proposed to ensure that people who make use of tax shelters are nevertheless subject to paying a minimum of income tax. People who purchase flow-through shares, people who purchase what are referred to as MURBs in the housing sector, and people who purchase shares that are tax deductible, are all using ways to avoid paying income tax.
The minimum tax was introduced to ensure that these taxpayers pay at least 17 per cent on income computed according to a different set of rules. This income, as explained in the legislation, will include tax shelters such as flow-through shares, MURBs and other types of tax shelters, all of which are to be reincluded in the alternative minimum income for the purposes of the minimum tax. The number of exemptions is very limited and includes only basic personal exemptions, charitable donations and a few other exemptions of this kind.
What is rather surprising, however, is that among the exemptions listed by the Minister of Finance in his technical notes and which we find in the legislation, we see that the taxpayer is allowed to deduct 50 per cent of his capital gains, which means that the only tax shelter that will not be included as income for the purposes of the minimum tax is the lifetime $500,000 exemption on capital gains.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is an insult to people's intelligence to propose a minimum tax and then, first of all, allow recovery of the tax over the next seven years and second, to subtract from income otherwise taxable for the purposes of the minimum tax, the lifetime capital gains exemption.
And something strange, that lifetime exemption on capital gains, for minimum income tax purposes again, comes under the same headings as personal exemptions, student exemptions and handicapped exemptions, the deduction for medical expenses, the deduction for charitable donations, the deduction available to people who took vows of perpetual poverty, the deductions in respect of certain social benefits, the deduction for due refunds of unemployment insurance benefits, the deduction for income averaging and finally in the total deductions they will include the lifetime exemption on capital gains on the same level as charitable donations, personal exemptions and exemptions for the handicapped.
Mr. Speaker, this is not good enough in my view. And this is why we are proposing in our Motion No. 14 an amendment by which, in computing the minimum income tax, the $500,000 lifetime exemption on capital gains would be treated the same way as other tax havens like flow-through shares, or MURBs, or benefits derived from investing in certain areas of economic activity.

And the reason why we are moving this at this stage is that during the previous discussion of the Bill, on the basis of the comments made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin), everybody on the Opposition side at least and many observers also realized that for the purposes of the minimum income tax, the $500,000 lifetime exemption on capital gains should receive the same treatment as the other tax havens, but we learned at the committee stage only, when we had officials before us, that what should finally be realized was that the capital gains exemption was also to be exempt from the minimum income tax. We believed that was unacceptable, and this is why we introduced the amendment in Motions Nos. 7 and 14.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed by the motion of the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). He simply wants to abolish the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. That is the only purpose of his motion. Yet, Mr. Speaker, to date, this tax exemption has proved useful economically. Small businesses and business people are all happy with this tax exemption, but the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides simply wants to abolish it.
I was listening to a television program not so long ago where he was publicly rebuffed and told that he was not being serious and that the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption was a good initiative.
He is at it again today since he wants to have this tax exemption abolished.
As for the minimum tax, he criticizes the fact that the amounts which may be payable in one year because of a very high income or salary can be recovered over a period of seven years. This is petty politics, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides is playing political games. I would like to give an example to explain the reason for this seven-year period. For instance, an artist might sell one, two or perhaps three paintings in one year. However, in a given year, he might be lucky enough to sell 25 and to have a very high business income for that year, but not for future years. If he has to pay the minimum tax that year, which he will have to do, this provision will be perfect to ensure that he pays his fair share of taxes.
However, what garantee is there that this same artist will not have a very low income in the next two, three of four years? The minimum tax is aimed at those who have high incomes year after year and who do not pay their fair share of taxes. Its purpose is not to tax someone who has a high income one year only.
Let us look, Mr. Speaker, at a young man from your constituency who has the good luck to sign a good hockey contract. He has a good income. However, in following years, either he is not considered to be a future hockey star or he has an accident which prevents him from playing. His career was
in hockey. It is true that he had a high income in 1986, but in 1987, 1988 and 1989, he will no longer have any income, but he would be taxed at a higher rate than other people.
Mr. Speaker, I think that we have to be realistic and this is why we set a period of seven years to adjust the tax rates of all taxpayers so that no one will be penalized compared with others. This is simply fair to all Canadian taxpayers and this is what we are doing with the Income Tax Act... I hear a Member on the other side laugh. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, they do not always understand.
A justice for the rich.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) introduced the minimum tax a year ago-I remember it clearly, I was here-his Leader rose in the House to congratulate us; now, one year later, he is laughing.
In principle, but not in practice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: One year later, Mr. Speaker, it is no longer good. It changes every day. They say that in the political world, one day is quite a long life. I realize now that for NDP Members, one year is a very, very long time, that policies and ideas change.
This is not a true minimum tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is a minimum tax, Mr. Speaker, and his Leader supported it.
No. Not at all!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All of this to say that this is the purpose of the legislation, and I respectfully submit that the two motions should be lost.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly remember that my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) had supported the principle of a minimum tax which had been introduced by the Government in its last year Budget. But what is significant is that because of the pressure from the New Democratic Party, the Conservatives have finally accepted to have a minimum income tax. But in reality, Mr. Speaker, it is not a minimum income tax but simply an advance tax which will be excused in the future, which means that it will be simply a tax pre-payment, an advance payment of the tax and not at all a real minimum tax.
What we are really faced with is a situation where high income people earning over $100,000 or $200,000 are not paying any income tax at all. Justice for low income earners and ordinary people who have to pay income tax year after year demands that rich people who have all kinds of benefits, who have legal counsels, real estate brokers and accountants at their service should not be able to avail themselves of all the loopholes in the tax system to avoid paying taxes.

This is the problem which the Parliamentary Secretary does not appear to understand. People who earn $250,000 a year are paying no tax at all while people who work as bank clerks, truck drivers and secretaries who earn $12,000 to $20,000 per year are paying a substantial portion of their incomes in tax. This is what we sought to have fixed by insisting that there be a minimum tax.
I remember the debate on television during the course of the 1984 election campaign. It was not the Progressive Conservatives who proposed a minimum tax. Nor was it the Liberals who proposed a minimum tax. It was the NDP. We proposed it and, finally, the other two Parties decided that they had better come on board. We now see their true stripes. The finance critic for the Liberal Party says that this is such a messy tax we might as well not have it at all. His Party really does not want there to be a minimum tax. The Government wants people to think that there is a minimum tax. But, in practice, because of the seven-year carry forward and because there are extra loopholes built into this minimum tax, it is not a minimum tax at all.

That is the reason why, Mr. Speaker, we introduced motions to delete the sections dealing with the minimum tax as proposed by the Government. We do not want to do away with the minimum income tax, but to give the Government a chance to reintroduce a really effective tax, a real minimum income tax.
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary did not mention people earning around $100,000 a year, for example. To start with, half of their capital gains would be exempt. Second, they would be able to take advantage of personal exemptions. Third, they are going to be entitled to a $40,000 deduction. To recapitulate, someone with a family, having an income of $100,000 a year and able to use all the loopholes to escape paying any normal income tax, would not pay 17 per cent in minimum income tax, but may be about half that amount, that is to say a minimum tax of $5,000, $6,000, $7,000 depending on the proportion coming from capital gains. But even that small amount is not really a tax, it is a deposit against any normal taxes the taxpayer might have to pay during the next seven years. In effect, Mr. Speaker, the only benefit for Treasury Board, for Revenue Canada, will be to receive $7,000 or $8,000 in 1987, for example, rather than in 1988, 1989 or 1994. That is the only result of this measure.
[DOT]	(1600)

That is not enough.
In the United States, that bastion of capitalism, tax reform proposals have been put forward by the Reagan administration, an administration which is certainly not a friend of this
Income Tax Act
Party, nor are we are friend of it. These proposals provide for a carry-forward of a minimum tax only in cases where it is judged that there has been a genuine tax deferred. For example, a corporation-and there is a corporate minimum tax in the United States-which defers tax by means of accelerated write-offs will in fact be able to take a tax credit for the minimum tax it pays in order that it can then pay off the tax that comes due later when the deferred tax becomes payable. However, if a tax is forgone in this country because of the tax-free exemption on capital gains, there is no such carry-forward at all. The American legislation, therefore, does not allow for three years of carry-forward as proposed by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), but for no carryforward at all where there is a total exemption from tax in the regular tax system. It seems to me that we should be looking at that kind of thing here.
According to the rules of the House, we will only vote once on each of these two motions, Nos. 8 and 15. While we propose to wipe out the seven-year carry-forward and then to review it in the context of an effective minimum tax, we will support the motion of the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides for a three-year carry-forward since it is better than the clause as it exists and it will indicate our opposition to the measures proposed by the Government.
Motion No. 15 deals with Clause 51 of the Bill. That is the clause which allows, among other things, for the deduction from the income assessed for the minimum tax of 50 per cent of capital gains on top of the regular 50 per cent exemption. In other words, while capital gains will become liable to minimum tax, they will be liable at half the rate of other income. That perpetuates the ludricous policy of the Government which allows $500,000 in capital gains to be tax-free.
The people who will benefit from the capital gains tax exemption are not ordinary taxpayers. They are people with high incomes. Perhaps 90 per cent of the benefit of that measure will go to the 5 per cent of the people who are top-income earners because they are the ones who invest and stand to make capital gains.
Capital gains on personal residences are not taxable in Canada because of the view that people will in fact roll that money forward and because one has only one principal residence at a time. Figures in today's newspaper suggested that only 17 per cent or 18 per cent of the population invests in the stock market and only a portion of that group receives any appreciable amount of capital gains. We are talking about a very small proportion of the population. Inevitably, those are the people who tend to be better educated, have better jobs and receive higher incomes. The ordinary people in my riding and the riding of Regina East, the farmers in Saskatchewan and others like that will have to pay extra taxes in order to provide a tax benefit to upper-income earners.
In addition, upper-income earners will have special privileged treatment when it comes to computing the minimum tax payable because some of their income came through the lifetime capital-gains tax exemption. These people are classed

December 17, 1986
Income Tax Act
as being as worthy as people who have taken a lifetime vow of poverty and receive a special income tax exemption for that purpose. I find that ludicrous. The amendment of the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides would at least do away with that particular objectionable and offensive part of the minimum tax. We will support that proposal. If we had the chance to do so, we would vote against the entire clause on the grounds that while the Government promised a minimum tax, and while we welcome the principle of a minimum tax, we did not get it.
We in Canada will really miss what is now in place in the United States and that is a minimum corporate tax. The use of preferred-shares financing and other dodges has allowed many of the largest and most powerful financial and industrial corporations in Canada to avoid virtually all corporate income tax. If it is a good principle that individuals should not be able to avoid paying a reasonably fair share of tax through the application of an effective minimum tax on personal incomes, that should be the case with corporate incomes as well. I regret the fact that the Government has not acted on that.

Mr. Speaker, when we are talking about the minimum tax let us not forget that the issue was raised during the 1984 election campaign by members of the New Democratic Party. The issue came up when the leaders were debating and, not to lose out on a good issue, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) immediately realized that Canadians on the whole are outraged by the fact that there are individuals who earn substantial income but year after year do not pay one cent of tax. The notion of a minimum tax became quite popular and the commitment was made by the Conservative Party that if elected it would introduce a minimum tax.
Today we see what type of minimum tax the Conservatives had in mind. It is a minimum tax full of loopholes. It is a sieve. As the Chairman of the Finance Committee so aptly put it, only unsophisticated taxpayers would be caught in this net. Certainly those who know how to plan their taxes and finances will escape paying one cent under the existing proposal for minimum tax.
I have here a copy of a newsletter entitled The Tax Letter which is put out by an accounting firm. It states: "Yes, you can beat the minimum tax," and it goes on to list several ways sophisticated taxpayers with the aid of accounting firms can avoid paying any minimum tax. The suggestions are numerous. Some tax shelters are still in effect. Interest deductions, tax havens, employer RPP contributions, business or investment losses and holding companies are some of the techniques that may be used to avoid paying the minimum tax.
A wealthy individual who has succeeded over the years in not paying any tax but does not quite have his finances in order this year will be hit with the minimum tax, but the Government gives him another loophole. He can claim those deductions in future years, in fact in seven years. It amounts to a deferral of exemptions. I would point out again that it is a
very ineffective minimum tax. I would be very surprised if indeed the Treasury collects any revenue under this proposal.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance pointed out that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced the minimum tax, the Leader and every Member of my Party welcomed the initiative. Certainly we understood it to be a commitment and recognition on the part of the Government that it was unfair to have Canadians earning substantial incomes year in and year out and not paying any tax at all. We welcomed that recognition, and we also took the Minister of Finance at his word when he stated the following:
What the minimum tax does is to prevent high-income taxpayers from using the capital gains exemption, alone or in combination with other tax incentives, to avoid paying tax in any one year.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary heard the Minister of Finance when he stated that the minimum tax would prevent individuals from using the capital gains exemption to avoid paying any tax at all.
Our amendment would put into force what the Minister of Finance promised the minimum tax would be when introduced. For the Parliamentary Secretary to defend the capital gains tax exemption in the minimum tax proposal contradicts what was promised by the Minister of Finance and what our Leader supported at that time.
When we see what the Tories mean by a minimum tax, can anyone blame us for not supporting the measure before the House? Surely everyone understands why we are not supporting that measure. Surely it is understandable to the Parliamentary Secretary and to other government Members why we are attempting to introduce some amendments to the piece of legislation, so that indeed it will become an effective minimum tax and there will be some tax justice and fairness in the country.
What about those individuals who live below the poverty line and began to pay taxes this year? I am referring to those persons who never paid taxes before. At least with a minimum tax, a sense of justice and fairness would be reintroduced into the system, and those persons earning from $50,000 to $100,000 or more per year would also pay a fair share in taxes. I urge the House to support the amendments.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 9 is meant to clarify the Government's intention concerning the federal sales tax child tax credit. For example, in the case of a separated or divorced couple, the way Bill C-23 was drafted when it was first introduced made it possible for both former spouses to claim the federal sales tax child tax credit.
We are moving this amendment because the intention of the Government is that the spouse who is keeping the dependent child or children should be the only one eligible for the $25 federal sales tax child credit. That is the purpose of Motion No. 9, and I urge Hon. Members to adopt it.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on Motion No. 10. As I said before in the House, granting a tax credit with respect to the federal sales tax is something entirely new in this field. It is an innovative approach which will make the tax system more objective. As a result of this measure a family earning less than $15,000 will be eligible for a tax credit related to items which it may have bought during the year and on which the federal sales tax may have been slightly increased.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this is important because 75,000 Canadian families are involved, and as early as next year they will be eligible for this tax credit, $50 for adults and $25 for children.
So this is important because we now have a system where sales tax can be increased for people with higher incomes who can afford to pay, and at the same time we can protect low-income individuals and their families. My point is that we had to introduce both the increase and the sales tax credit.
Mr. Speaker, I submit, with respect, that Motion No. 9 should be approved in order to restore what the Minister of Finance intended when he brought down the Budget, which was that per spouse or per child, if you prefer, a federal sales tax credit of $25 would be available, and that the federal sales tax credit proposed in the Budget by the Minister of Finance

December 17, 1986
Income Tax Act
in February 1986 be maintained. I feel this is a progressive measure that shows the Conservative Government's concern for low-income families, and at the same time opens up new possibilities for the application of the Income Tax Act and related Acts. It shows this Government is creative and is capable of thought and action. It shows that we can have a Canadian tax system that will be fair to all Canadians. That is what we have sought, and I think that up to now, Mr. Speaker, we have been successful.
I shall, if I may, quote some comments by the well known C.D. Howe Institute, Mr. Speaker, which mentioned in a recent report:
The Government's record in identifying priorities over the past year or so has been good. The February 1986 Budget introduced a fiscal plan to reduce the deficit and stabilize the debt ratio at below 60 per cent by the end of the decade.

Mr. Speaker, the C.D. Howe Institute is known as a nonpartisan group. These are people who analyze and look at what the federal Government is doing in the fiscal area, in its Budget and what it is doing for the Canadian economy and the individual provinces. I think that what it says here and what I just quoted is an accurate reflection of the mandate we received in 1984.
They go a little further, Mr. Speaker and perhaps I may quote, this is called Fiscal Responsibility and Tax Reform, and it mentions the $2.5 billion increase in the deficit announced by the Minister of Finance in September. It says here, Mr. Speaker:

In the Institute's assessment, this deviation from the target is acceptable, provided that the Government continues to demonstrate its commitment to deficit reduction in the medium term. No single deficit number is the dividing line between responsible and irresponsible fiscal management.

And it goes on like this, in that they understand the problems the Canadian Government has had to cope with in the West and the additional needs and expenditures with which it was confronted. However, Mr. Speaker, the important thing is that for the second consecutive year, we managed not to increase our spending. The increase in this year's deficit will be due, not to an increase in spending but to a drop in Government revenues. That is something, Mr. Speaker, that had not been seen in Canada in the last ten years. It is important to stress that, since we are discussing Bill C-23 that provides for most of the tax schemes which we introduced in February 1986 and which necessarily worked their way through the Canadian economy and the economies of all the provinces, of your constituency and of the beautiful constituency of Trois-Rivieres which you know of course. By the way, things are going well in Trois-Rivieres, we have a low 10 per cent unemployment rate. But this again is due to the concrete steps taken in the May 1985 and the February 1986 budgets.
I will conclude on this Mr. Speaker, by urging the House to pass Motion No. 9 as rapidly as possible, and to reject Motion No. 10.

Mr. Speaker, our amendment asks for the rejection of the Government motion. In essence what the Government has done is, it has taken one thousandfold from the poor and by this measure will return a fraction. The Government is proposing a rebate to "your average family" of two parents and two children. It will return to those people $150 if they earn $15,000 or less. By the time the family earns $18,000 it will get nothing back.
You have to consider, Mr. Speaker, that since the Government came to power it has taken some $845 per year out of the pockets of your average family in increased sales and excise taxes. The Government is willing to pay back $150 to low-income groups. That is cynical to say the least. What happens to the people in the income brackets of $18,000, $19,000 and $20,000 a year, again a family of four trying to make ends meet? These people very often in this day and age are living in tremendous insecurity and desperation. Their lifestyles are not like those of us in the House of Commons. Their lifestyles are not like those people in the Finance Department. These people live in genuine economic insecurity and fear. They are the working poor. Very often they have great difficulty maintaining permanent jobs. They are often the first to lose their jobs. They are perhaps living in the the most difficult period in our history. Very often they are trying to raise families under extremely difficult situations. They have had extra tax burdens placed on them by the Government since it came to power, not only through hefty increases in sales and excise taxes but on vitamins, non-prescription drugs, chocolate bars, soft drinks and a host of other items. As well there have been changes to the Income Tax Act. The other week I heard testimony from the National Council on Welfare. It presented a graph. The line on the graph keeps going up. Starting in 1985 for the first time earnings equal to half the poverty line in Canada will be taxed. In other words, people earning half of what is considered to be the poverty line will start paying income tax. That line continues upward from 1985 to 1986 to 1987 to 1988 to 1989 to 1990 and so forth. It is true though that the Government has introduced some measures that will soften the blow to the very poor. When you deduct the sales tax credit and the marginal increase in benefits for children from those increased taxes you will find that the very poor are worse off than they were before.
The other part of the equation is the benefits that the well-to-do have received from this Government. The Financial Post of March 8, 1986, analysed the effect of the Conservative Government budgets on the $40,000, $60,000, and $150,000 income groups. The $40,000 group will end up paying marginally more, around $800, in taxes from 1984 to 1987. The $60,000 group will end up paying roughly $1,200 less in
December 17, 1986

taxes in 1987 than they did in 1984. The $150,000 group will end up paying some $6,000 less. I call that obscene. There is no other word for it.
The Government tries to dress up this inequity by pointing to the $150 it will pay to a family of four. This is not only unfair, it is unjust. That is why we are asking now, as we intended in committee, that the minimum tax credit be $200 for an adult rather than $50, and $100 for a dependant, rather than $25. That is less than what the anti-poverty groups have called for. They asked that the tax credit for an adult be $400, and $200 for a child. They feel that at that level the poor will be protected from the increase in the cost of living due to these sales and excise tax increases put forward by the Government. That is also why we have no alternative but to oppose this part of the legislation. By doing so we hope to raise the awareness of the Government which has been socking it to the poor. For heaven's sake, redress the injustice in the next Budget and allow a decent tax credit for poor families.

Mr. Speaker, on Motion No. 9 introduced by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin), which adds details to the definitions of people entitled to the income tax credit, I have no objection and I do not think it is worth the trouble discussing it at length. Indeed, the new version might be more specific and prevent interpretations that could prove costly or unfair. So, as far as Motion No. 9 is concerned, I have no objection and we will support it immediately.
As far as Motion No. 10 is concerned, I do not understand it, Mr. Speaker. I do not understand it in the sense that it proposes to remove clause 42 entirely .
I understand the objective of the mover and of the New Democratic Party, but if this motion were adopted, there would be no tax credit whatsoever to reimburse the sales tax which have been dramatically increased by the Conservative Government in the last two years. This tax has gone from 9 to 12 per cent, which is an increase of 33 per cent. It is not surprising that the Government should feel somewhat embarrassed by its harassment of low-income families and that it would want to provide a tax credit.
I agree with the mover of motion No. 10 that the tax credit as proposed is completely insufficient. As the previous speaker has just pointed out, at the meeting of the Committee on Finance when representatives of the Canadian Welfare Council came to express their views, it was clearly established that to compensate, not future increases, but those which have already been proposed and implemented by the Conservative Government, we would need a tax credit of $400 per adult, while Clause 42 of this bill only provides for tax credits of $50 per adult and $25 per child. This is totally insufficient.
This tax credit is not only insufficient, it is also embarrassing. If I were sitting to the right on the Government benches and had to vote on this measure, I would be embarrassed to propose such a thing when all organizations, including Government agencies such as Statistics Canada, have set the
Income Tax Act
poverty line for a family of four in a major urban centre at $21,000 and the tax credit being proposed is only $50 per adult and $25 per child based on a maximum income of $15,000. This represents a $6,000 difference for a family of four. It is senseless. The amount is totally insufficient and I am surprised that the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres did not say so in his comments earlier.
Mr. Speaker, we are put in a difficult position because, on the one hand, if we support motion No. 10 now before us, there will be no tax credit whatsoever. And on the other hand, if we vote against the motion, we feel we may be supporting a Government proposal that is totally inadequate. Basically, we are caught between two evils, but I believe it is still better to have a totally inadequate provision than no provision at all. And this is why we are goin to support Motion No. 9 but reject Motion No. 10, not because we agree in any way with the amounts indicated but, quite the opposite, because if we were to support Motion No. 10, we would in effect preclude all form of support, all form of help to compensate families at least in part for the dramatic tax increases that have been imposed by the Tory Government over the last two years. So we will support Motion No. 9 and reject Motion No. 10.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment very briefly before the vote, just to say that the Government's proposal is so inadequate there is no way we could support it. The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides said he and his party felt squeezed, and for that reason they were going to support the motion even though they saw it as totally inadequate. On this side of the House, this utter inadequacy leads us to say simply that we should scratch that clause from the legislation, in order that the Government may put in place a more adequate provision. Now, it is not the Opposition's right or privilege to propose measures that entail expenditures, and we therefore have no way of introducing a motion to put in place an adequate provision for the sales tax credit.
It is therefore one of two things: Either we support our proposal, our motion, to defeat that clause and allow the Governement to bring in another proposal, or else we tolerate an intolerable situation, as proposed by the Liberals.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to Hon. Members that I hope they will vote with us and reject that inadequate measure, for the main reason that if the Government intends to bring in a business transaction tax with a small compensation for low income families, it is very clear that, under that Government proposal, their idea of what is adequate and acceptable is so unacceptable that the new business transaction tax will be totally regressive.

Mr. Speaker, Clauses 42 and 43 cut the corporate tax break from 46 to 43 per cent. In addition, the Government is widening, by another 1 per cent, the tax reduction for manufacturing businesses. In essence, the Government is taking a head start on its proposals for tax reform. It took significant steps to broaden the corporate tax base in the Budget of February, 1986. It did so by eliminating the 3 per cent inventory allowance deduction, by eliminating investment tax credits, and by tightening the rules on limited partnership tax shelters.
The problem is that although the Government earned a certain amount of revenue by broadening the tax base, it promptly used that revenue to cut corporate tax rates. The consequence is that when we get to tax reform in the new year, as we have been promised we will, there will be nothing in the kitty to finance other changes in taxation.
I believe most Canadians hold the view that the corporate sector has been undertaxed and that we need to consider very seriously whether corporations should not pay a greater proportion of the total federal Government tax revenues. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary knows that that is the public perception. Polling by the Department of Finance itself has indicated that.
The share of taxes paid by corporations has fallen during the last 10 or 15 years. However, rather than trying to redress that problem, the Government and the Department of Finance have taken the view that corporate tax changes should be "revenue
neutral". That means that anything gained by broadening the base should promptly be given back to the corporate sector through rate reduction. We think that is wrong. We think the Government should hold its bets with regard to the ultimate levels of corporation tax until the entire picture of tax reform is before Canadians.
Second, a number of the tax expenditures which are being eliminated were established initially to achieve certain objectives and worthy goals. Groups from all across the spectrum have concluded that the use of the tax system for that purpose is ineffective. I was on television a few months ago with the head of the Canadian Federation for Independent Business. I was most surprised to learn that he was saying much the same as I was. We had grave doubts as to whether the tax loopholes which were designed to further worthy goals were working and we felt they should be removed.
You can be darn sure, Mr. Speaker, that if the corporate sector is denied tax loopholes, it will be looking for grants, subventions, and other forms of assistance. An example is that which is happening at the GM plant in Quebec. There is talk of a substantial interest-free loan which amounts to a grant. That will not be seen through the tax system, but it will have to be paid for in one way or another. We are going to have increased amounts to pay in terms of industrial incentives.
In certain circumstances an NDP government would be prepared to look at such a policy in the context of an over-all industrial strategy. The money must come from somewhere. A revenue-neutral tax reform for corporations means that you have given away the money you may have redeployed into grants and other forms of incentives. The Government has taken the view that in broadening the base corporations should be assessed lower tax rates. Money given to the corporate sector to assist with worthy objectives through grants or other above-the-table payments will have to come from elsewhere. It will obviously have to come from either the transaction tax or income tax which is paid for by ordinary Canadian taxpayers. Once again, the Government's priorities are distorted. The effect of its giving an immediate tax cut to corporations will be to impose a larger tax burden on ordinary Canadians.
The marginal rate on corporations is now 46 per cent. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary knows perfectly well that the effective rate on corporations is well below that, perhaps 20 or 25 per cent. My belief that if you demonstrably increase the effective rate on corporations it will be possible to cut the marginal rate was confirmed by the visit of the Finance Committee to Washington to study tax reform. However, the Government has this reversed. It is cutting the marginal rate on corporations without demonstrating that there is a substantial and effective increase in the effective rate in corporation tax.
I believe, therefore, that the Government is acting in error. A sceptic or cynic would say that while the Government cloaks itself in the mantle of tax reform, it is in fact finding a way of delivering, under the guise of a modernized tax system, a
December 17, 1986

further benefit to its friends on Bay Street and St. James Street.

Briefly, Mr. Speaker, 1 simply want to say that the Government is acting prematurely when it reduces the corporate income tax from 46 to 43 per cent, and when it widens by another 1 per cent the tax reduction for manufacturing businesses. First of all, there is precious little indication that such tax incentives really create jobs. In addition, broadening the tax base does not in my opinion, justify a tax reduction until the Government unveils the entire picture of its tax reform.
The Government seems to think it is a good idea to have a revenue-neutral tax system for corporations, which means that if revenues are increased as a result of a broader tax base, corporate tax rates should be promptly reduced instead of considering the possibility of transfering part of the personal tax load to the corporate sector.
Mr. Speaker, we the NDP members agree with most Canadians who believe that corporations do not pay their fair share of the total tax revenues in Canada, and we think that corporations should indeed contribute more.
We also believe that instead of simply letting the Government reduce corporate tax rates we should wait to see whether or not the effective corporate tax rate will increase.
The United States reduce the marginal rate at the same time as they raise the effective rate. If we had evidence that the same thing is being done in Canada, then we might be more inclined to accept the Government proposition. But since no such evidence has been forthcoming either in committee or in the House, we will oppose these measures until such time as the Government discloses its entire tax reform and gives Parliament an opportunity to scrutinize it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not quite sure that you were pleased to recognize me, but I should be quite prepared to yield to the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides if he is ready-
In this case, Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides.
Mr. Speaker, I have just heard the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) say that he is against helping the GM plant in Quebec; on the other hand, I read recently that a great friend of his, Mr. Bob White, was fully in favour of it. I suggest, therefore, that the Hon. Member should consult his friend about this and report to us. But to return to motion no. 11 standing in his name, Mr. Speaker, when we talk about reducing the corporate tax rate, there would be at the same time a broadening of the tax base. In this connection, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre has been fair and emphasized what we have done about this in our last Budget. However, when he talked about reducing the corporate tax rate, Mr. Speaker, we must take the entrepreneurship into
Income Tax Act
account. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre has taken the view that corporate tax changes should be "revenue neutral". I am all for that, but we should not overlook the fact that corporations in Canada should have enough of after-tax revenues to reinvest them.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Centre referred to our Bay Street friends. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I have no friends on Bay Street, but I do have some on Desforges Street in Trois-Rivieres-
You act as though you had friends on Bay Street.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
-and it is those people from Desforges Street, from the constituency of Trois-Rivieres, from your own constituency and from the Laval-des-Rapides riding who reinvest. They are the ones responsible for the current excellent economic situation in Canada. If we want those people to reinvest, we cannot tax away all of their profits. We have to help them and this is what we are doing. The response has been excellent. It is too bad that the New Democratic Party cannot understand it. This is how it is. Our businesses must have enough money left to reinvest.
In Trois-Rivieres, car dealerships are doing very well. They are expanding. Trois-Rivieres dairies invested large amounts last year. I hope that they will soon be reinvesting to change their fleet of trucks. They can do that, Mr. Speaker, because they have enough money left after taxes to go on, to expand, to create new jobs, to make the economic wheels turn. Whether we are speaking about our own region, the province or the whole country, it is something that has to happen.
Some say that we should be increasing the corporate tax rates, but I think that this is a bad idea. If the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre told me that we should see to it that all companies pay their fair share of taxes, I would perhaps be more willing to discuss the matter with him. However, let him not say that we should tax businesses more. I therefore respectfully submit that motion No. 11 should be defeated.
As for motion No. 12, which would simply eliminate the manufacturing processing tax credit, I believe that the same principle applies.
In the case of motion No. 13, unfortunately, 1 did not have the opportunity to hear the arguments of the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides. I shall wait to hear his views, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I will comment more substantially on Motion No. 13 which has been regrouped for debate.
I would just like to comment briefly on the two preceding motions which would delete two clauses in the Bill.
Mr. Speaker, I agree generally with the principle of broadening the tax base to lower the effective tax rate, and I

December 17, 1986
Income Tax Act
think the Government's objective in this respect should be twofold. First, it must ensure that companies pay their fair share of taxes. Easy to say, but very difficult to define.
The second point the Government will have to bear in mind when setting these tax rates is the competitive position of Canadian companies in the production of goods or services, as compared with Canada's competitors on the international markets. It is easy to say: this person or group of persons or group of companies has to pay more. However, I believe our objective must be to maintain a high level of employment, which will be difficult to achieve if Canadian companies are taxed more heavily than their American counterparts who, in many cases, are only thirty or forty kilometers away, and who, because of the free movement of goods between the United States and Canada, can easily enter the Canadian market and vice versa. So our competitive position must be maintained.
In Bill C-23, the Government has abolished exemptions and broadened the base, and this has a direct impact on business. However, reducing the tax rate over a given period is done in such a way that despite what the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Vincent) said earlier, this year, Canadian businesses will pay slightly more taxes because on the one hand the base has been extended and immediately implemented and, on the other hand, rates have been reduced on a two, three or four-year period so that in the meantime, businesses will pay slightly more income tax.
Mr. Speaker, my proposal contained in Motion No. 13 is aimed at striking out some lines in Clause 49 the purpose of which was to rescind several investment credits in some areas of the country. Those investment credits have been useful because they have enabled some remote areas to take advantage of investments which they would not have obtained without that help extended through the tax system for businessmen who had decided to invest in some prescribed areas, that is as set under the regulations.
At present, Section 49 will rescind for all practical purposes investment tax credits which will be solely limited to some areas such as Cape Breton and other parts of the country but in a very limited fashion. This means we will no longer have a regional development policy in Canada, since the only instrument the Government had left in place was the tax credit that is now going to be abolished by Clause 49. I am not saying that the tax credits we had in the past were the answer to all our problems. Certainly not. But at least our tax legislation provided some encouragement for businessmen and women who wanted to invest in remote areas. In its February Budget and in Bill C-23, the federal Government has submitted that these policies no longer meet the desired objectives. They are being abolished but not replaced. Not a single regional development policy has been developed by the Government for this country, not a single one, as far as our businessmen and women are aware. And now, the Government is going to destroy one more instrument without providing for a replacement.
From the very outset, when I first arrived in the House, my concern was the attitude of a Government that wanted to apply one rule and one rule only: the principle of market forces. I agree that our economic system should continue to be based on a market economy, especially since we live on the North American continent and belong to international organizations for the liberalisation of trade, and so forth, but in a country like Canada, I don't think we can envisage the harmonious economic development of this country without a regional development policy for industrial investment and for air, railway and marine transportation.
This country was built around regional development policies, and since it came to power, the Conservative Government has been steadily demolishing the regional development instruments that were in place, however imperfect they may have been and however great their shortcomings. I would agree if they had said they were going to replace them with better policies. I am willing to sit down anywhere, on any committee or here in the House, to discuss the parameters of such policies. However, I cannot agree with abolishing instruments, however imperfect they may be, if they are not replaced. If Motion No. 13 is not approved, this means that investment tax credits applicable to remote areas will be abolished, at a time when the Government's budget for regional and economic development assistance has already been cut by several hundred million dollars. The Government is on the point of abolishing various transport services because of the sacred law of the market and we shall end up with a country eroded by a lack of consistency and the absence of an economic policy to facilitate the East-West movement of goods. What we shall have instead will be a North-South movement and with free trade, there will be a multiplication factor of ten. This country of ours was built on regional development policies which were based first on railway transport and then on other tools of regional development. This might seem very simple, Mr. Speaker, but if yet another tool of regional economic development is abolished and is not replaced by anything, an economic situation will develop in Canada where there will be two or three prosperous major centres, perhaps Toronto, and up to a point, Montreal, and even then, we have to wonder about Montreal with what happened in Eastern Montreal and what is now happening in Sainte-Therese, and so on. Finally, there might be two or three centres of activity and all the rest will be disadvantaged peripheral regions which the Conservative Government will have abandoned by abolishing one after another all our economic development tools which, while not being perfect, have been built up over the years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Debate on Motions Nos. 17 and 18. The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau).

Mr. Speaker, if we refer to debates which took place during the 1984 election campaign and to statements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the House or outside the House during debates or in answer to questions asked by newsmen before TV cameras, we remember that the two leading stars now on the national scene-the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance-had made very firm commitments concerning taxation.
Speaking of the Prime Minister, for instance, I have here a quotation from the Toronto Sun of 1984, and I will read what is reported as being the comments of the Prime Minister, which were never denied, I might add. I quote:

"Prime Minister, Brian Mulroney, says he does not favour higher personal income taxes to reduce the swelling federal deficit because Canadians are already over-taxed".

Mr. Speaker, I should think that at the time all Canadians agreed with this statement made by the present Prime Minister of Canada.
Later on, the same Prime Minister of Canada said, and this time I am quoting from the Toronto Star:
In The Toronto Star of June 1, 1985, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is quoted as saying that Canadians are already over-taxed. He stated that Canadians are already paying a pretty hefty bundle for their government services and that they feel they are paying enough. He concluded by saying that that view is not without its support in government, private industry and labour circles.
2222

December 17, 1986
Income Tax Act
I think most taxpayers and voters would have agreed, and would agree today, with the words of the Prime Minister. I could also quote the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who said that taxes were already too high.
What this Bill does is to impose another huge increase in taxes not just directly or indirectly but through a surtax. The amazing thing is that if this Bill is adopted, for part of 1986- and I suppose it will be because of the Tory majority-and when we fill out our tax returns in 1987, we will have three surtaxes to pay. It takes a special clause in Bill C-23 to fix that. There was the 5 per cent surtax mentioned in the Budget of 1985, as well as the 10 per cent surtax. We will now have a 3 per cent surtax over and above the other two.
I say that enough is enough, particularly for those who are in financial difficulty. I refer to those who live below the poverty line as established by Statistics Canada, or any other group which has studied this matter. In committee, representatives of the National Council on Welfare explained the difficulties low income earners face. For example, they told us that the poverty line for a family of four in cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver and Winnipeg is $21,000. Everyone knows that it is not easy for a family of four to live in a large city with an income of $16,000 or $17,000 per year. Now the Government will impose an additional 3 per cent surtax on these people. In this way a family of four will have to pay $24 in 1986, because it deals with only six months of the year, and $47 more in 1987. When people fill out their income tax returns for 1986 they will realize that they have to pay $200 to $500 more in tax because of these surtaxes.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, this Bill will add a third surtax and what we would like to do, what I would ask the Government- besides, this, came very close to being introduced directly in the House, because the Chair's deciding vote in Committee would have been required to defeat the motion I had proposed at that point. So I call upon Conservative Members to think this over well, as some of their colleagues did in committee. If the Government feels a 3 per cent surtax is absolutely needed, at least it should not apply to people living below the poverty line. They already find it hard enough to pay their regular taxes, without the Government slapping on them a 5 per cent tax plus another 3 per cent tax for the last six months of 1986.
I call upon Hon. Members to show compassion before the holiday season, and the Minister of State (Finance) probably is in this House. I would ask him to show some compassion for those who must live below the poverty line and to see that at least the surtax imposed by his colleague the Minister of Finance does not apply to them.
This is why the motion before the House, although we could have specified the amounts, proposes that, in order to leave some more elbow room to the Government, Clause 67 be amended so that the 3 per cent surtax Cannot be charged to those who live below the poverty line, which could be established by the Government by regulation. What I have in mind
is that the Government should follow the recommendations and data provided by Statistics Canada, a Government body, so that the poverty line for income tax purposes agree with Statistics Canada. But if, for different reasons, a somewhat lower level were prefered, let at least the principle prevail that people below the poverty line should not be charged that 3 per cent additional surtax that is levied by Bill C-23 under Clause 67.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words against the motion of the Hon. Member. This time of Christmas charity when we think of those less fortunate than ourselves can be no better time to raise the point raised by the Hon. Member. I wish to speak very seriously to the point he makes.
First, I would like to remind the House that over the course of the last two or three weeks people have been receiving the prepayment of the child tax credit, a meaningful amount of money. Depending on the size of the family the prepayment can be anywhere from $200 to $500. This money will help these families at this time of year.
There is also the refundable federal sales tax credit which is geared to low income Canadians. Both the prepayment of the child tax credit and the refund of the federal sales tax credit mean that we are compensating those who live below the poverty line. These are important matters. As well, there is the disability allowance which has been increased. We have also added to the qualifications for it. People who are in need in this country have been looked after through these measures.
With respect to the motion of the Hon. Member, I know that when he makes his point he seeks to Find a place at which we can stop the surtax. It would be logical for him to suggest, as he has, that that place is the poverty line. The problem with his proposal is that it would create an administrative nightmare. More important, it would not be fair to those with incomes just above the poverty line to have to pay the tax and the surtax while those below the poverty line pay nothing. The poverty line is itself an arbitrary barrier.
So you tax the poor instead.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
If we put this motion in context with all the other budget measures for lower income Canadians that the Government has taken, we have to say that the motion cannot stand.
It is important for other reasons as well, reasons which affect all Canadians, including low income Canadians. Once again, this is a measure to decrease the deficit. It will produce revenues of $1.2 billion. That is in the interest of all Canadians. If control of the deficit helps us to come to terms with and build confidence in our economy, then that will lead to investment. Then small business and large business will be able to create jobs for Canadians. That is really what we have been producing. It is the most important way to attack the problem of poverty.
December 17, 1986

In the spirit of the Christmas season, I remind the House of these things that we are doing for low income Canadians and I must ask that the motion be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has invoked the Christmas spirit. Let me lay clearly before the House the record of the Government's treatment of low income families. I will quote from the report of the National Council on Welfare which says:
Giving and Taking: the May 1985 Budget and the Poor argued that, despite the increase in the child tax credit, many poor and all middle-income families with children will receive lower net child benefits as a result of the partial indexation of family allowances and the reduction in the children's tax exemption.
The report goes on to say:
The analysis takes into account the following changes: the partial indexation of family allowances, the gradual increase in the child tax credit and the lowering and partial indexation of its turnover point, the gradual decrease in the children's tax exemption, the partial indexation of personal tax exemptions and tax brackets, the elimination of the federal income tax reduction, the raise in tax deduction limits for private pension plan and RRSP contributions, the imposition of federal surtaxes and the introduction of the refundable sales tax credit.
We do not include the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption or the impact of increases in federal sales and excise taxes (which affect the cost of a number of goods and services but not the disposable income of families and individuals).
Taking all that into consideration, the council has found the following:
A two-earner couple supporting two children on earnings equal to three-quarters the estimated poverty line ($16,280) will lose over $1,200-
That is over five years.
-while a family with combined spouses' earnings at the low-income line ($21,700) is behind by more than $2,100. A couple earning $25,000 loses $2,500 in disposable income.
Note that the high-income couple with $100,000 loses only $2,182- significantly less than middle-income families. In fact the family earning just $21,700 loses about the same amount of disposable income (close to $2,200) as the $100,000 family which earns five times as much.
The Minister tells us that the Conservative Government has been good to the poor. We have found that for the first time, people with incomes at half the poverty line will be paying income tax because of the tax measures of the Government. For the Minister of State for Finance to place on the record the claim that the Government's tax policies have been good and beneficial to the poor and then not to hear rebuttals to that is shameful.
The record shows that the Government has benefited well-to-do income-earners while it has put extra tax burdens on the poor. Keeping in mind the spirit of Christmas, I find it shameful that people who live on incomes of half the poverty line are being taxed for the first time by the Conservative Government. People who try to scrape out an existence with incomes of three-quarters of the poverty line will see their taxes dramatically increased as will people whose incomes are on the poverty line.
Income Tax Act
For the Government to claim that it has been fair to the poor and has given them extra tax measures is obscene. Not only has the Government cut back on the programs that helped the poor but it is extracting more money from the poor. As far as the poor people of Canada are concerned, this Government will go down in the history books as being one of the meanest Governments.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on third reading of Bill C-23. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I have already had the opportunity to insist on the significance of Bill C-23 and the need to adopt it before the end of 1986 for all Canadian men and women.
In short, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-23 is to streamline the Income Tax Act while rendering the tax system more fair and equitable for all Canadians. This legislation must be seen in the context of the economic recovery which started when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Conservative team came to power on September 4, 1984. It will help Canada's economic activity, first by decreasing corporate taxe rates, and second by extending the corporate tax base. It also is aimed at establishing a minimum income tax for all Canadians with a certain level of income each year and who pay little or no income tax.
As I pointed out again this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party had expressed his agreement when we tabled our notice to establish a minimum income tax for individuals-
On the principle.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
-on the principle. On the other hand, the legislation must be enacted before the end of 1986 because it also is aimed at increasing the allowable RRSP deduction from $5,500 to $7,500 a year as early as 1986. This, Mr. Speaker, is something important for all working people who want to invest more money in view of their forthcoming retirement.
There is also a social fairness aspect to Bill C-23, as you certainly have noticed it Mr. Speaker, with the sales tax credit.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, this is an excellent piece of legislation following in the wake of an excellent Budget, and I would urge the House to enact it as rapidly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I find it hard to understand that a Bill under which nearly $1.2 billion will be drawn from the pockets of Canadian taxpayers can be labeled a good piece of legislation. This is why we are going to oppose the Bill on third reading, without calling for a recorded vote in view of the Government majority. But we certainly are going to ask that it be carried on division.
This Bill will increase taxes for thousands and thousands of Canadians by more than $1 billion.
December 17, 1986

This Bill is contrary to the statements that have been made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) during and after the 1984 election.
As a result of this Bill and Bill C-14, which was adopted on division by the House earlier this week, the Canadian taxpayers will pay an extra $1.2 billion. The total amount of new taxes for the fiscal year 1986, as a result of the 1985 Budget and the 1986 Budget, will be $6 billion.
Since the Minister is in the House, let me quote what he said on August 28, 1984. He said:
We have no intention of raising income taxes to Canadians. What we have to do is get down government.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Up the taxes.

Up the taxes and get the Canadian taxpayers down is the reality. The Minister introduced $6 billion in new taxes after he made those remarks in 1984, before the election. Of course, he was making promises in order to obtain votes.
On March 1, 1985, after the election, the Minister of Finance said on CTV Question Period:
I don't want to increase taxes-I think we have a good deal of scope on the expenditure side to deal with the deficit problem. A tax increase, certainly a general tax increase, puts a dampening effect on the economy and I don't want to see us do that.
Since then we have seen the Budgets of May, 1985 and February, 1986, with $6 billion in new taxes. If anyone should put his seat on the line it is the Minister of Finance who made those statements before and after the election and then increased taxes by $6 billion.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak to this Bill briefly because it is close to Christmas and Members want to leave the House. First, I want to talk about the process.
This Bill was initiated in the Budget of February 26, 1986. There was a Ways and Means motion in June, but the Bill did not come before the House for debate until December 8, just over one week ago. The Government cut short debate on second reading and jammed the Bill through in the committee without allowing the opportunity to hear from outside groups or organizations who may have wished to testify on the Bill.
The Bill has come back to the House and now, on third reading, we are allowed three or four minutes to speak because it is very close to Christmas. That is not a good way to deal with tax legislation. While it may be necessary to pass such legislation before the end of the year, I suggest that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) should introduce such legislation into the House at least one or two months before the deadline, if such a deadline is necessary.
In just over two years of office the Government has raised taxes on ordinary Canadians by $1,350 per family per annum.
Income Tax Act
The Government has never challenged those figures. The Minister of Finance is here but he is not challenging them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: I challenge them.

Although the Government is moving toward tax reform that broadens the base and lowers the rates, Bill C-23 narrows the base with unsupportable concessions on pension contributions and increases on RRSP deductions.
Not only is there an ineffective minimum tax, the Minister, despite his promises in 1985, has slipped in a loophole with respect to capital gains so that if there is any minimum tax on capital gains it will be borne at half the rate of other forms of income.
The sales tax credit is inadequate, particularly when one considers that the Government intends to use a sales tax credit to promote its business transfer tax. Corporation taxes are being cut in advance of tax reform and, rather than placing a surtax on the rich, it has been replaced with a surtax on every taxpayer, including taxpayers who are below the poverty line.
Canadians did not vote for that kind of tax system in 1984 and that is why the Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin) has joined our caucus. The people of Quebec and all Canadians voted for real change in June, 1984. They did not get it from the Conservatives but they will get it from the New Democrats, whether it is on taxation, jobs or the creation of social justice for all Canadians.
